items.title: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure
items.summary:
Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million. 

“We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.” 

Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew quickly, until Booking .com and the big hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes said. 

The founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he said, referring to the $12.4 million the company had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014. 

It was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he said. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the big one—the company that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.” 

Leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards…
items.t: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure

items.title: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO raises the stakes for its enterprise AI business
items.summary:
Good morning. Founded just five years ago, Anthropic is a powerhouse in AI. Now, it’s making its public debut on Nasdaq.

The company is expected to start trading today under the ticker ANT, with the deal expected to close on Friday. Anthropic announced yesterday that it had priced its IPO at $83 per share, with 980 million shares on offer—about 956.4 million from the company and 23.6 million from existing shareholders.

The offering price is above the initially indicated range of $70 to $78 per share and values the AI company at $1.5 trillion, Fortune’s tech editor Alexei Oreskovic writes . The company said it will receive no proceeds from existing shareholders’ sales. Underwriters have 30 days to buy up to 147 million additional shares.

Founded in 2021 and led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic develops the Claude family of AI models and products, including Claude Code and Cowork. Krishna Rao joined Anthropic as the company’s first CFO in May 2024.

The offering also gives some of Anthropic’s seven cofounders an opportunity to sell a portion of their holdings. Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei, and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan are among those selling small portions of their equity, Oreskovic reports. Read more here .

Accelerating growth in its enterprise business is a priority for the company. “Since Anthropic was founded, we have focused on building AI for the enterprise,” Rao wrote in a LinkedIn post in September. He added: “We will keep building for the use cases that matter most to businesses.”

According to Anthropic’s IPO disclosures , as of Sept. 30, more…
items.t: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO raises the stakes for its enterprise AI business

items.title: Unless you’re building a data center or have a side hustle, you’re significantly worse off than last year, according to the Fed
items.summary:
Walk into a grocery store, park, or gas station, and you’ll notice prices across the U.S. keep climbing. On top of that, the Federal Reserve’s latest minutes suggest that unless you’re in two very niche groups of consumers, you’re probably markedly worse off in terms of income in 2026 compared to last year.

By its very nature, inflation erodes spending power as prices rise. But in a balanced economy, when inflation is at its target of 2%, those increases are offset by income growth, so consumers can still afford goods and services without seeking additional income or eating into their savings.

But in 2026, inflation has been well above the 2% target. The latest inflation readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics came in at 3.7% over the past 12 months, through September 2026. However, in addition to prices rising above the central bank’s 2% target, Fed minutes from the latest Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting showed wage growth for most industries lagged well behind price increases.

The affordability conundrum facing households is therefore twofold: Not only are prices rising quicker than consumers can reasonably expect, but any increases to their income are coming in well short of the new demands on their purse strings. 

The Fed minutes from the meeting ending October 28 read that most participants “judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the committee’s 2% inflation objective.” 

Some sectors are posting wage growth, the notes adding many members “observed that shortages of skilled workers needed for…
items.t: Unless you’re building a data center or have a side hustle, you’re significantly worse off than last year, according to the Fed

items.title: An obscure Marxist critic who died fleeing the Nazis saw ‘aura farming’ coming 90 years ago—and why you can’t afford to see the Knicks or Taylor Swift
items.summary:
Gen Z calls it “ aura farming .” Live Nation calls it “being there.” The hottest idea in the AI economy belongs to a Marxist critic who wrote his ideas in exile, never saw a royalty, and died tragically—a total obscurity in his own time.

Walter Benjamin was obsessed with the subject of the “aura” in the 1930s, and he thought mass reproduction would kill it. 

“That which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art,” he wrote. “Even the most perfect reproduction of a work of art is lacking in one element: its presence in time and space, its unique existence at the place where it happens to be.”

His 1935 essay, “ The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction ,” was barely seen during his lifetime, and picked up increasing steam in the ensuing decades , at first in leftist European journals and then its 1968 English translation. Hannah Arendt, a great journalist and critic in her own right, who coined the phrase “ the banality of evil ” and covered Adolf Eichmann’s trial for the New Yorker , selected it for the collection Illuminations , and wrote the introduction.

The German-Jewish critic fled Germany in 1933 and spent most of the rest of the decade in exile, much of it in Paris, working on an unfinished history of the city’s 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades, forerunners of the mall. (He was really into arcades.) In September 1940, he crossed the Pyrenees into Spain with a small group of refugees. Franco’s police told them they would be sent back to France, and the next morning Benjamin was found dead in his hotel in…
items.t: An obscure Marxist critic who died fleeing the Nazis saw ‘aura farming’ coming 90 years ago—and why you can’t afford to see the Knicks or Taylor Swift

items.title: GoDaddy chief strategy and legal officer: AI agents still have a trust problem. The solution is waiting
items.summary:
The age of AI assistants is almost here. Soon, we’ll delegate tasks like comparing flight prices or managing routine household purchases to agents acting on our behalf.

That convenience could transform the digital economy. But it also raises a basic question. How will those systems know which agents, services, and businesses they can trust?

The answer will shape whether the next generation of the internet remains open and interoperable—or becomes fragmented across a handful of competing platforms and proprietary ecosystems.

We have solved a problem like this before. In the early days of the internet, navigating online was like trying to find a business in a city with no street names or storefront signs. The destinations existed. But users needed to know the underlying IP address of each server.

The Domain Name System, or DNS, changed that. It transformed the internet from a confusing network of numerical addresses into a navigable web of trusted identities. Endings like .com, .gov, and .edu helped organize the landscape. More importantly, websites could present stable, human-readable names of their own.

Names like Wikipedia.org and Amazon .com told users exactly where they were going. These names also gave businesses and institutions a unique, durable, and universally accessible online presence, one which many built into the global brands we recognize today.

DNS also helped establish trust. Without such a system, a name like Amazon.com could never have functioned as a trusted commercial identity. A user might have seen the label in a browser and still had little…
items.t: GoDaddy chief strategy and legal officer: AI agents still have a trust problem. The solution is waiting

items.title: I’m the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally. Here’s what business leaders are wrestling wit
items.summary:
For the past year, the conversation about enterprise AI and security has fixated on what region the models come from. It is a fair question. But as the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally, I often speak with the increasing number of business leaders adopting open models. Where their models come from is not the question that keeps them up at night.

What they worry about is more simple. They ask questions like, “Where does my data go when I use these models?”, “Who can see it?”, and “How long is it kept?”

These questions matter more than ever right now, and not just because of the latest string of hacks over the past month, including PHP2Shell which left millions of websites around the world vulnerable, but because of how AI is being used in businesses. Coding agents, security tools and internal assistants send enormous amounts of company information to a model: source code, internal documents, customer details, the context of a team’s daily work. Not only is this highly sensitive information for a business, but it’s also extremely valuable to anyone who wants to train a model of their own.

AI leaders are already bracing for what comes next. NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang made it a feature in his keynote at GTC Berlin, and Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer, recently warned that conditions would get worse before they improve, urging business leaders to take action. That action starts with knowing where company information goes when AI is used.

Most companies assume a vendor either protects their data or it…
items.t: I’m the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally. Here’s what business leaders are wrestling wit

items.title: Adecco CEO: Only 19% of workers think their bosses get AI’s toll. This is the leadership test of this generation.
items.summary:
Only 19% of workers say their leaders are empathetic to the effects of change. That finding, from our latest Global Workforce of the Future research surveying 40,500 workers across 36 countries, should make every leader stop and think.

The AI debate is entering a more serious phase. The first wave focused on what AI could do. The second focused on massive jobs replacement. What matters now is more pragmatic: which organizations can turn AI into lasting productivity, resilient operating models and better work? How do leaders prepare themselves to accompany their people and organizations to create value?

AI’s productivity prize will not come from rolling out more tools alone. It will come from redesigning work, skills, governance and operating models. Technology may be the catalyst, but workforce readiness will determine how much value companies actually create.

AI needs to happen with people and not to people. This is the leadership test of this generation.

Work is being reshaped, not erased 

The evidence gives us reason for optimism, but not complacency. Labor market data tells a more nuanced story than the job apocalypse headlines of earlier this year. AI is not triggering a collapse of human work. It is reshaping how work is organized, performed and governed. Employment remains resilient across most advanced economies – OECD employment rates remain near record highs. Large-scale AI-driven job losses just have not materialized – with impact on tasks rather than jobs. Most companies are still at the beginning of their AI journey, experimenting with tools and trying to…
items.t: Adecco CEO: Only 19% of workers think their bosses get AI’s toll. This is the leadership test of this generation.

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

items.title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy checks his watch and ends the interview on the spot if you can’t answer his go-to question, says $55 billion EA cofounder
items.summary:
Amazon’s CEO Andy Jassy has one go-to interview question, and if you can’t answer it on the spot, he’ll look down at his watch and end the interview. At least, according to Bing Gordon.

Gordon was a founding exec at $55 billion EA Games—where he helped create The Sims , the game that had millennial girls around the world hooked—and Audible. He also served on Amazon’s board of directors from 2003 to 2017. 

And one time, he was sitting at dinner with fellow Amazon execs, including Jassy before he became chief exec, when the conversation turned to who had the best go-to interview question. 

“My go-to interview question is, ‘What would it take to keep you in a company like ours for 20 years? And who’s your business hero?’ And Andy Jassy had a better one,” Gordon told Fortune . “He said, ‘Mine is: what’s your strategy for constant learning?’”

Gordon instantly listed the various ways he learns, from reading books to watching people—which Jassy said was an instant green flag.

“He said: ‘Good, you know it off the top of your head. When I ask that question, if somebody goes, what do you mean? He says, as far as I’m concerned, the interview is now over, and I look at my watch and try to figure out how to get out of it.’”

Fortune reached out to Amazon for comment.

How to respond to unusual interview questions and get ahead in your 20s

items.title: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier

The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours…
items.t: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier

items.title: Waymo says its robotaxis crash far less than humans. California just called them an ‘imminent hazard’ and pulled them off freeways
items.summary:
Waymo says its robotaxis are involved in far fewer serious crashes than human drivers. California regulators now say its cars are an “imminent hazard” on the freeway.

On Nov. 11, the California Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo from operating or testing its driverless cars on freeways after several vehicles entered an active construction closure and another incident in which a Waymo tried to get around California Highway Patrol cars running a traffic break. Waymo has since paused driverless freeway rides in all its markets, including Phoenix, Miami and Austin, though it is still testing on freeways with specialists behind the wheel.

“Right now we’re looking at this technology. You get in it, you expect it to work perfectly,” Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT’s AgeLab who studies automated vehicles, told Fortune . “We shouldn’t.”

The DMV said three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame on Nov. 5. Then the agency cited the separate incident involving Highway Patrol vehicles in San Francisco, ultimately resulting in the agency declaring Waymo’s freeway operations an “imminent hazard to public safety,” in a statement.

It’s the second time this year Waymo’s freeway service has gone dark. Similar incidents in May prompted an earlier restriction and corrective actions, but the DMV said Waymo’s vehicles continued entering active construction zones despite those changes. Waymo paused freeway rides nationwide then, too, and brought them back gradually starting in late July.

“Safety is at the foundation of…

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

items.t: Energy price cap rise: how to beat the January hike

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

items.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
items.summary:
Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill

  • Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers

  • Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal?

  • UK inflation rises to 3.6%

Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households.

The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
